# aeneid-069 (IX.530–620) — drafter's notes

36 units; `make_units.py` runs clean (no LINE COUNT / TOO LONG / NEWLINE / ENDING warnings). `t` comes only from `A.cut`; no `sc`.
Every note is under 140 words (longest 124, the 569–572 unit).
Paragraphs: 530, 590 (both `p: true`; each note opens "A new paragraph in Greenough.").
Speech marks: Turnus to Lycus opens and closes inside the 560–562 unit (`“Nostrasne… manus? ”Simul`); Numanus's taunt opens
in the 598–599 unit (`“Non pudet`) and closes in the 619–620 unit (`ferro.”`). 2 “ / 2 ” in t; l and i carry the same marks
on the same units.

The 569–576 killing list (one sentence, eight lines, commas only) is split at the comma after `sagitta,` (572): 569–572 and
573–576, four lines each. The 573–576 note says `sternit` (571) still governs.

## Misprint calls (rule 5b; t as printed, l/i corrected, note opens with the print's reading)

- **9.561 `manus? ”Simul`** for `manus?” Simul` (closing mark joined to the next word, as 7.560, 8.404, 9.22). The unit
  560–562 therefore also carries *Simul adripit… revellit.*; the short speech is opened and closed in it.
- **9.567 `agere`** for `aggere` (dropped letter). *agere* ("to drive") gives no sense with *fossas… complent* and does not
  scan (`fōssās | ăgĕrĕ` fails); Greenough prints *aggere* everywhere else (16 other times, incl. 9.43, 9.769); the Latin Library
  has `aggere`. Unit 567 (*invadunt… complent;*), cut on its own.
- **9.601 `adegit`** with no mark before the capital `Non` (602): a question (*Quis deus… quae… dementia*) that can only end
  with `?`. l/i read `adegit?`. Same handling as 8.137 / 9.289 (left as a note, not a rule-5 source fix, because the
  printed page could not be checked). If the page prints `?`, add it to the source and re-pin aeneid-069 under rule 5;
  then only the note's opening changes. The unit runs 601–602 to `Ulixes:` because `adegit` cannot end a unit.
- **9.620 `Idaeae sinite`** with no mark between them: a break is certain (*Matris Idaeae* closes the drum-and-flute clause,
  *sinite* is a new imperative). l/i read a semicolon. Same doubt about rule 5 as above; whether Greenough printed `;` or `:`
  could not be checked. Note opens "The print has no mark after 'Idaeae'… a misprint for a stop (a semicolon is read here)".

## Kept as printed (doubtful readings / Latin Library variants noted where the sense changes)

- **9.579 `infixa est lateri manus`**: Greenough's reading (the hand pinned to the side); the Latin Library has `infixa est
  alte lateri` with no `manus` (the arrow fixed deep). Both scan. Noted in the 578–580 unit.
- **9.584 `Matris luco`**: Greenough's reading, kept (he capitalises it; cf. *Matris Idaeae* 619). The Latin Library has
  `Martis` ("grove of Mars"). Noted in the 581–585 unit; the note does not identify the Mother (could be the mother of the
  Palici or Cybele — I did not assert either).
- Orthographic variants ignored: 550 `adstare`/`astare`, 561 `adripit`/`arripit` (noted only as Greenough's `adr-`), 578/580
  `volnus/volnere`, 591 `fugaces`/`fugacis`, 611 `vires`/`viris` (mentioned in passing in the 610–611 note).
- Greenough's habits noted, not misprints: `adfixit`, `adstare`, `adripit`, `adlapsa`, `adsueta`, `adsuetis`, `inruit`,
  `volnus`, `volnere`, `sperasti`.
- Ilioneus spelt with one l at 569 (as everywhere except 9.501's `Illionei`); nothing to flag.

## Bracketed lines and half-lines

None in 530–620.

## Set pieces

None in this part (checked against the conventions list).

## Advisory: none

Ordinary battle killing (men crushed and impaled under the tower, Lycus torn from the wall, Privernus's hand pinned by an
arrow, the son of Arcens's head split by a sling-bullet). No sexual violence. Consistent with 067/068.

## Scansion worries (for the reviewer; not my job to write scan-fixes)

- **553 `inicit`**: consonantal i after a prefix, `īnĭcĭt` (in-yicit) as a dactyl. Scanner blind spot.
- **569 `Ilioneus`**: Greek *eu* one syllable: `Īlĭŏ | neūs sāx | (o) āt quīn | gēn tī | frāgmĭnĕ | mōntīs` with
  `sax(o) atqu(e) ingenti`.
- **567 `agere`**: as printed the line does not scan; the scansion should follow `aggere` (as 8.323 `tutis`/`tutus`).
- **584 `Symaethia`**: the line seems to need `Sȳ-` long (`cō Sȳ | maēthĭă | cīrcūm`); I am not sure of the quantity.
- **600 `conubia`**: needs `cōnūbĭă` in the fifth foot (`nūbĭă | pōscūnt`); check the scanner does not treat `-bi-` as
  consonantal.
- **609 `versaque iuvencum`**: no elision (consonantal i of *iuvencum*); the note says so.
- **571 `Corynaeum`**: `gēr Cŏrў | naē ūm | stērnĭt Ă | sīlās`.
- Usual blind spots: *Teucri* absent; initial Ae- none; *Maeonio* 546 (`Maē-ŏ-nĭ-ō`).

## Attributions made from memory or inference (please check)

- Checked against the Latin in source: Corynaeus a Trojan at 6.228 and alive at 12.298; Liger fighting for Turnus at
  10.576; Capys at 1.183 and as founder of Capua 10.145; Caeneus 6.448; Ascanius's stag 7.496–499; *aggere* elsewhere.
- Unchecked: Iliad 12 (the Trojan assault on the Greek wall) as a general model for 530–534; Iliad 12.41–48 (boar/lion whose
  courage kills it) for the Helenor simile; Iliad 22.308–310 (Hector swooping like an eagle on a lamb or hare); Iliad 2.235
  (Thersites, "Achaean women, no longer Achaean men") for 617.
- Myth/background from memory: Troy taken twice (Hercules and Laomedon, then the Greeks); the Palici as twin Sicilian gods
  near the Symaethus; the ancient belief that sling-bullets melt in flight (I did not name Lucretius or anyone); *vetitis
  armis* explained as a slave's son forbidden to serve (given as "perhaps"); Cybele's eunuch priests; Dindymus and
  Berecyntus as Phrygian mountains of Cybele; *ferrugo* as a dark red dye; *manicae* as a mark of softness to Romans.
- 572 *hic… hic* taken in order (Liger javelin, Asilas arrow); the sides of Liger and Asilas left open in the note.
- 594: *dicitur* taken as the personal construction with *Ascanius* its subject.
